contents: # The shell (uhifadhi/shell-module) — what this installation looks like: the
# document, the page frame, the sidebar and top bar, the navigation seams and
# the theme every module's pages mount into.
# NOTHING BELOW IS REQUIRED. All three keys have defaults, and the config tree
# is closed, so an unknown key fails loudly rather than being ignored. A fresh
# installation with this bundle and nothing else boots and SERVES: a branded,
# themed, navigable shell with an empty sidebar. There is no database, no
# migration and no entity behind any of this — the shell draws, it does not
# remember.
# THERE IS DELIBERATELY NO KEY LISTING NAV ENTRIES, AREA TABS OR MODULES. Those
# arrive as data through the two seams at the bottom of this file, because a nav
# declared in YAML is a nav no permission check ever reaches.
shell:
# The wordmark beside the brand mark in the sidebar. Yours to change: the
# shell cannot know what this deployment calls itself.
brand_name: Uhifadhi
# Where the brand mark links. The shell is installed BY an application and
# cannot know its route names, so it takes one — and tolerates its absence:
# until a route by this name exists, the mark links to `/` rather than
# failing the page. That is what makes the first boot of a new installation
# work before it has grown a home screen.
home_route: dashboard_index
# What a visitor who has NEVER chosen a theme gets: light, dark, or
# `system` to honour what their operating system already says. All three
# are real answers — `system` is not a synonym for light.
# Whatever this says, the choice is applied by an inline script in the
# document head, BEFORE the first paint, so nobody is shown the wrong
# palette for a frame. A link may override it for one view with `?theme=dark`.
default_theme: light
# THE TWO LINES THIS RECIPE CANNOT WRITE FOR YOU — and unlike the seam's, they
# are genuinely OPTIONAL. The shell renders without either of them; it just has
# nothing to put in the sidebar, which is the honest picture of an installation
# that has nothing in it yet.
# They belong in config/services.yaml rather than here, because both are service
# wiring and neither is a setting:
#   services:
#       # WHAT GOES IN THE SIDEBAR. Implement
#       # Uhifadhi\Shell\Contract\NavigationSourceInterface and return
#       # NavSection/NavItem value objects. Your application has the areas, the
#       # viewer and the permission voters; folding those into "these rows, in
#       # this order" is a reading for a person on a page, and it is yours.
#       # GATING IS YOURS TOO: the shell holds no authorization service and asks
#       # nothing about the viewer. A row somebody may not have is one you do not
#       # return — there is no "hidden" flag, because a hidden row is a row that
#       # leaks its existence to whoever reads the HTML.
#       # The tag is written by hand because a reusable bundle's services are not
#       # autoconfigured. More than one class may carry it; a module bundle can
#       # contribute a row of its own the same way.
#       App\Shell\HostNavigation:
#           tags: ['shell.nav_section']
#       # WHERE THE VIEWER IS, AND WHICH SIBLING SCREENS IT HAS. Implement
#       # Uhifadhi\Shell\Contract\AreaShellSourceInterface — tabs() for the strip
#       # above a page, place() for the middle segment of its title.
#       # An ALIAS, not a tag: two things claiming to know where the viewer is,
#       # is exactly the disagreement this bundle exists to prevent. Exactly one
#       # tab must be lit, and a screen somebody may not reach is ABSENT rather
#       # than greyed out — a disabled tab tells a person a screen exists and
#       # they are not trusted with it, which is worse than not mentioning it.
#       shell.area_shell_source: '@App\Shell\AreaShell'
# AND ONE LINE IN YOUR TEMPLATES. The shell's stylesheet carries the theme
# tokens and its own furniture; it is linked by the document, first, so your
# application's stylesheet can override it. Your pages reach the shell by
# extending one of its three frames:
#   {% extends '@UhifadhiShell/page.html.twig' %}   {# a normal page #}
#   {% extends '@UhifadhiShell/shell.html.twig' %}  {# full-bleed: no page frame #}
#   {% extends '@UhifadhiShell/document.html.twig' %} {# print/export: no furniture #}
# WHAT THE SHELL DOES NOT SHIP, and you do: the two Stimulus controllers its
# markup names — `sidebar` (the collapsed rail) and `sidebar-tree` (folding),
# plus `theme` for the toggle. A bundle cannot contribute an importmap entry, so
# the markup is here and the behaviour is yours. Until you add them the shell
# renders correctly and simply does not fold — attributes with no controller
# behind them are inert, never broken.
# The shell's routes (uhifadhi/shell-module) — one line, and it is yours.
# The shell ships one route: the welcome page, named `welcome`, at `/` — the one
# screen a fresh installation has before it has grown one of its own. The bundle
# DEFINES it and loads it nowhere. This import is what makes it reachable, and
# this file belongs to YOUR application.
# THAT IS THE WHOLE OF THE SHELL'S CLAIM ON A URL, and withdrawing it is one
# edit. The day this installation has a real home screen, point `/` at it here —
# or delete this file and let whichever module owns the front door claim the
# address. Nothing in the shell depends on the route name or on the route
# existing; nothing is left behind.
# `debug:router` shows what you are replacing.
shell:
resource: '@UhifadhiShellBundle/config/routes/welcome.php'
